cue: Much like your own sight, with a sharp centre and three kinds of colour sensor.

cpd.note: the sharp centre of a monkey with a fovea; the pick of one value for the whole picture is the app's

M.note: three cone types with peaks gathered from three different primates, used for primates in general

PRIMATE_TRI.note: the 430 peak is from a cynomolgus monkey, the 530 peak from a howler monkey and the 561 peak from a marmoset; the combination is the app's

cpd.note: the grey mouse lemur, a small nocturnal primate

fov.note: a person's 180 scaled by the ratio of a Pan-like 115 degrees to a human 136.1 degrees, from a skull model

sat.note: owl monkeys have one cone type, so the picture is drawn in grey

rows: A marmoset's cone mosaic could carry about 30 cycles per degree at the fovea, about what you manage. A stumptail macaque with an intact fovea resolved 1.4 minutes of arc, about 21 cycles per degree. We keep the sharpness at 30.

A grey mouse lemur resolves about 4.9 cycles per degree, and another estimate from its retina gives 4.2. A common marmoset has about half the acuity of a person. For a mouse lemur we blur the picture to 4.9.

Macaques have three kinds of cone, as you do. A cynomolgus monkey has a blue-sensitive cone near 430 nanometres. A howler monkey has a pigment near 530 and a marmoset one near 561. We combine these three peaks, so the colours come out close to what you see.

Male marmosets have two kinds of cone. Capuchins are two-cone or three-cone depending on the animal, and howler monkeys have three. The three-cone matrix stands for all of them, so some animals would see less colour than we show.
Owl monkeys are the only night-active monkeys. Their retinas have a single type of cone, so they lack colour vision, and their fovea is only rudimentary. We draw their view in grey.
A model built from chimpanzee and bonobo skulls gives a widest sideways reach of 115 degrees with the eye turned outward, against 136.1 degrees for a person. We scale a person's field by that ratio.

Neurons in a macaque's visual cortex respond to the small differences between the two eyes' pictures, which gives stereo depth. A marmoset can also focus over more than 20 dioptres. We leave depth as your camera gives it.

One value of sharpness stands for every monkey with a fovea, and one three-cone colour matrix built from peaks of three different primates stands for all primates. The chimpanzee field of view is worked out by scaling, and owl monkeys are drawn with no colour. No record gave a pupil shape, a dim-light gain or a field of view for other species, so those stay as a person's.
